correctness.rationale: For each nonzero component, the trace pairing imposes exactly one independent linear equation because a nonzero matrix entry is detected by a matrix unit; a zero component imposes none. Thus support size alone determines the orthogonal-set cardinality. Removing the zero tuple and, precisely for self-orthogonal vertices, the vertex itself gives the two degrees in each support stratum. Both types occur because E_12 is nonzero self-orthogonal and E_11 is not. Summing the two degree multiplicities over each support size gives the elementary symmetric polynomials in the nonzero factor cardinalities. The number of degree pairs gives k, the ratio of graph order to minimum-degree offset gives q^k, and Viète reconstruction gives every q^(n_i^2)-1. The packaged replay checks the trace-kernel premise, one complete product graph, and several multi-factor reconstructions.

originality.rationale: The 2024 full survey explicitly states as open Problems 2 and 3 the trace graphs of direct products with unequal matrix sizes and of arbitrary finite products over an integral domain. The closest prior degree theorem concerns a single common matrix size over a commutative ring, while the closest prior isomorphism theorem recovers only the underlying ring cardinality and matrix size in that one-size setting. The accepted theorem solves the common-finite-field n_i>=2 case of Problem 3 and recovers the entire size multiset from the graph degree distribution. Targeted database and web searches, including post-2024 searches, did not locate an equivalent elementary-symmetric reconstruction theorem.
residual_risks: An equivalent direct-product theorem may occur under orthogonality-graph or bilinear-form terminology not captured by trace-graph searches.

value.rationale: The theorem solves a broad finite-field subcase of an explicit direct-product open problem rather than a single finite example. It gives a rigidity result: the graph degree distribution alone recovers the field order and every simple matrix-factor size. The elementary-symmetric reconstruction works uniformly for an arbitrary number of factors and therefore meaningfully advances both the two-factor and multi-factor problems.
